newsitem.title: USA: Hard-hit Great Plains buried by another blizzard.
newsitem.headline: Hard-hit Great Plains buried by another blizzard.

text.p: Blinding snow stranded drivers in the Great Plains Wednesday and bone-chilling cold froze cattle already stressed by a parade of winter storms.
The latest blizzard to strike the Northern Plains made roads impassable and heightened the hardships suffered by residents who have been buried in towering snowdrifts.
Police in Grand Forks told marooned motorists to wait by their cellular phones in their cars as ploughs tried to clear snow-blocked roads for rescuers.

"It's our weekly blizzard," Grand Forks police dispatcher Amelia Sebenaler said resignedly. At least one accident within the city limits Wednesday caused several injuries and dozens of deaths were blamed on one of the worst winters in memory in the plains, where several motorists were found frozen behind the wheel and many people suffered frostbite.

In Minnesota, the weekend deaths of six snowmobilers brought to 23 the number of deaths this winter on the machines, with most of the accidents attributed to alcohol and not the weather. A 10-year-old boy died when he was struck by an allegedly drunk snowmobiler while crossing the street.

"Some snowmobilers continue to give their sport a black eye by punching the throttle or hitting the bottle," said Leo Haseman, director of the enforcement division at Minnesota's Department of Natural Resources.

Deep snow and biting cold proved fatal to thousands of cattle and weakened animals were losing their calves as well. Some ranchers were unable to get feed and water to their herds and cattle losses in the Dakotas were estimated to be as high as 140,000 head, but officials could not count the carcasses because of the snow.

Bowdle, South Dakota, rancher Cal Sandmeier said he used a giant snowblower attached to a 220-horsepower tractor to clear 30-foot drifts and gain access to his herd, but he worried that his neighbours did not have such equipment.
His nearly 350 cows were scheduled to calve in April. Just one had lost a calf, but other ranchers reported a slew of aborted calves.
"This is strange country," Sandmeier said, referring to the bout of harsh weather that followed a brief thaw earlier this week.

The fast-moving storm was forecast to sweep across the Great Lakes, possibly piling up more "lake effect" snow on coastal areas, then sweep into Canada. Warmer air drove thunderstorms across the Ohio River Valley to the East Coast.
